text: Odysseus Does Not Tell the Crew About Scylla: May a Leader Conceal That Some Will Die to Keep Everyone Rowing?
When Circe explains the way ahead to Odysseus, she offers him no safe route.
One way leads past rocks that clash together.
Great waves, flames, and shattered timbers mingle there, and scarcely any mortal ship has ever passed through intact.
The other leads through a narrow strait.
Scylla lives on one side.
From her cave high in the cliff she thrusts out six heads, each capable of snatching a person from the deck.
On the other side is Charybdis.
She swallows the sea together with the ships upon it, and not even the sea god can save anyone at that moment.
Circe's advice is very clear:
Keep close to Scylla's side and row past as quickly as possible.
Better to mourn six companions aboard than to lose everyone together.
Odysseus asks:
Could he put on his armor and fight Scylla off?
Circe answers:
No.
This is not an enemy a mortal can defeat through prowess.
Stopping to fight will only let her thrust out her six heads again and take another six people.
Here, escape is the bravest course.
This story can easily be reduced to an arithmetic problem:
Six people, or the whole ship.
Odysseus chooses to sacrifice fewer people to save more.
But “chooses to sacrifice six” is too hasty.
He does not pick out six names from among the crew.
Nor does he abandon, for the sake of efficiency, a route on which just a little more effort would bring everyone through safely.
Even he does not know whom Scylla will seize.
He faces a strait already described by divine guidance as having no way through without loss.
If Circe's words are true, the six deaths are not a cost he arbitrarily adds to the voyage, but an almost inescapable danger on the less destructive route.
Beyond this danger that cannot be removed, however, there is something Odysseus truly does decide for himself:
Whether to tell the crew.
He chooses not to.
What makes this decision especially sharp is that slightly earlier in the same book, Odysseus has just said almost the opposite.
As the ship approaches the Sirens, he gathers his companions.
He says:
The prophecies Circe told me should not be known to just one or two of us.
I will tell everyone, so that knowing the danger, we may either escape or face death.
He then explains how the Sirens' song will tempt sailors, and tells the men how to stop their ears with wax and tie him to the mast.
Here, knowing the danger is a condition of carrying out a shared undertaking.
Everyone needs to follow the plan precisely.
The crew knows why they must not listen.
They also know that even if Odysseus begs, they must not untie him.
Information allows them, before the danger arrives, to restrain the Odysseus who will later lose control of himself.
Yet once the ship has left the Sirens and begins to approach Scylla and Charybdis, the same principle that knowledge “should not be confined to one or two” is no longer followed through.
Smoke, huge waves, and a roar appear over the sea.
The crew is so terrified that the oars slip from their hands.
The ship stops moving forward.
Odysseus makes his way along the deck, reassuring them one by one.
He says that the danger before them will be no more terrible than the Cyclops's cave.
It was courage, judgment, and cunning that allowed them to escape before.
One day, they will look back on this ordeal too.
Then he orders everyone back to the benches to keep rowing.
He also orders the helmsman away from the smoke and great waves, close to the cliff on the other side.
The crew obeys.
Here the poem tells the reader directly:
Odysseus does not go on to tell them about Scylla.
He fears that if his companions know she is waiting to seize six of them, terror will make them stop rowing and crowd into the hold.
And if the ship stops, Charybdis may swallow them all.
So this is not simply an act of deception.
Odysseus does not conceal the truth to gain some secret advantage for himself.
Nor does he send others to die in his place while he remains safe.
He judges that complete information will destroy the whole ship's last remaining ability to act.
The men have already just stopped rowing at the sight in the distance.
If they also learn that six heads will randomly snatch people from above, each may instinctively leave the deck and try to avoid exposure.
Yet rowing is precisely what gives the ship a chance to pass through quickly.
In these circumstances, telling the truth does more than return the decision to everyone.
It may also leave too little time to carry out any decision at all.
Being informed usually helps people take part in shaping their own fate.
Here, however, it may immediately destroy the conditions for a shared escape.
This makes “leaders should be transparent” an insufficient answer.
A leader may sometimes hold information that the members of a group cannot all bear at once.
In a fire, battle, voyage, or rescue, spelling out every worst-case possibility at the most dangerous moment may cause panic that blocks exits, defeats instructions, and increases the harm.
Concealing information or delaying an explanation may genuinely serve to protect.
But having a protective reason for concealment does not make it costless.
The crew continues rowing without knowing the specific danger posed by Scylla.
They have no chance to ask:
Why choose this side?
Are six losses truly unavoidable?
Is there another formation we could use?
Are we willing to take this route together?
Circumstances may give them no time to discuss it.
But having no time to obtain an answer cannot be rewritten as their having already given one.
Odysseus himself does not hide.
Forgetting or defying Circe's explicit warning, he puts on shining armor, takes two long spears, and stands at the bow looking for Scylla.
He wants to protect his companions when the monster appears.
This shows that he does not calmly accept that “six deaths will do.”
He still hopes that heroic ability can alter the prophecy.
Yet Circe has already told him that stopping to fight will only bring more deaths.
His weapons save no one.
Instead, they show how hard it is even for the person with complete information truly to accept:
Some dangers cannot be resolved by confronting them bravely.
Odysseus keeps the crew uninformed so that they will continue carrying out the only workable plan.
Yet inwardly, he still refuses to acknowledge fully what this plan is powerless to prevent.
The ship enters the strait.
Every eye is drawn to Charybdis.
The water boils, exposing black sand in the depths.
The crew goes pale, afraid that the whole ship will be sucked down.
While they look in that direction, Scylla thrusts out her six heads from the other side.
She snatches six of the strongest and most powerful companions.
Odysseus looks up and sees their arms and legs struggling in the air.
The six men call his name for the last time.
They are not calling to Circe.
Not to fate.
Nor to an abstract “majority.”
They call to Odysseus.
Because he is the one who knows.
The one who gave the order to row.
And the one who brought the ship into this strait.
Their cry cannot prove that his decision must have been wrong.
Even if everyone had known in advance, Scylla might still have taken six men.
If the crew had indeed abandoned their oars and hidden, the outcome might have been worse.
There is no textual evidence that disclosing the information would have created a route on which everyone could be saved.
Yet the six men's cries still prevent their leader from completing his account with “the others survived.”
Numbers can explain the choice of a smaller loss.
They cannot make the smaller loss a nameless one.
The six are not “a group of six.”
They are companions who have just escaped the Sirens together and rowed together at sea.
And they are the strongest men aboard.
Their deaths may have preserved more lives.
That does not reduce those deaths to the correct answer in a calculation.
Necessity can mitigate blame.
It cannot cancel a relationship.
If Odysseus had no other route at all, he would still need to mourn.
If concealment truly prevented the whole ship's destruction, he would still need to acknowledge:
I knew something you did not.
As a result, you took no part in the decision.
Six of you bore a cost that we could not discuss together.
The stronger a leader's reasons for deciding on everyone's behalf, the less he can pretend afterward, when the decision succeeds, that he merely experienced an accident along with everyone else.
For his relationship to the outcome is one the others do not share:
He knew in advance.
Knowing does not mean being able to control.
This matters too.
Odysseus knows that Scylla will take six men, but not which six, and he cannot stop her.
Equating “knowing beforehand” directly with “deliberately killing” would misrepresent limited foresight as an all-powerful decision.
He does not hand particular companions over to the monster.
Nor does he gain a private benefit from their deaths.
He tries to fight, and afterward calls the sight the most pitiful of all his experiences at sea.
So he is not a ruler who deals with people through cold arithmetic.
But it is precisely because he is not all-powerful that his concealment needs limits all the more.
When someone who cannot control the outcome decides what others should not know, he undertakes an immensely weighty judgment.
Such judgment needs at least several limits.
Does the concealment last only until the danger has passed?
Is there truly no way to explain that takes less away from them?
Has the decision-maker too quickly labeled possible objections as panic in order to preserve his own authority?
Is he willing afterward to acknowledge the full disparity in knowledge, rather than credit every success to his leadership and every failure to unavoidable fate?
If a similar situation arises later, will the community be allowed to remake its rules in light of the earlier loss?
The Odyssey does not turn these questions into an institutional system.
It gives us only an extreme scene.
But an extreme scene can reveal the limits of an ordinary principle:
“For your own good, I am keeping this from you” may sometimes be true.
And precisely because it may be true, it calls for greater caution than an obvious lie.
The crew are not always passive subjects of Odysseus's commands.
On the Sun God's island, they will collectively oppose continuing the voyage at night, and later slaughter the sacred cattle in defiance of the ban.
Before the Sirens, they carry out the plan strictly, even tightening the ropes when Odysseus asks to be untied.
This is a group capable of judging, protesting, and making mistakes.
Odysseus does not withhold the news of Scylla because they are inherently unentitled to know.
He does so because he judges, at that moment, that knowing will deprive them of their ability to act.
This essay cannot prove on the text's behalf that his judgment must be right.
It can only acknowledge that the facts give it substantial support:
Smoke and great waves have already made the oars fall.
But this is still Odysseus's judgment about how his companions will react, not his companions' own answer.
After the six men die, the remaining crew sit down on the next island and weep.
They remember the companions Scylla has taken until sleep overcomes their mourning.
This shows that the community does not immediately write off the minority because the majority has survived.
But the voyage must still continue.
Grief cannot keep the ship stopped forever.
This is the hardest thing when no way through without loss exists:
Going on seems to make use of an outcome bought by the dead.
Staying in place may make all the losses greater still.
No action can erase the deaths that have already occurred.
The only choice still available is how to keep “we must go on” from becoming “we need no longer answer.”
Facing Scylla, Odysseus is neither someone freely choosing a sacrifice nor an unknowing sufferer in exactly the same position as an ordinary crew member.
He occupies the space between:
Knowing more.
Able to decide more.
Still unable to control the most important outcome.
This position gives leadership responsibility its heaviest form.
If he were all-powerful, he should simply remove the danger.
If he knew nothing at all, he could only suffer with the rest.
Someone who knows some things and can decide some things, yet cannot prevent all harm, must bring others into the consequences amid uncertainty.
He therefore cannot vindicate himself through the outcome alone:
Most of us lived, so the decision was right.
Nor can he vindicate himself through intention alone:
I meant to save people, so the concealment needs no explanation.
Circe says:
Better to mourn six than to lose the whole ship.
Her words give a reason for the choice of route.
They do not complete Odysseus's entire judgment about whether to tell his companions.
In the end, he chooses to keep everyone rowing while he alone knows what waits on the high cliff.
Perhaps there is no better way.
But “there is no better way” is no license to act lightly.
It means:
The decision-maker must regard the unavoidable loss as his own concern, not as a part of a successful plan that can be passed over.
The six companions call his name at the end.
That cry is not necessarily an accusation.
It may simply be people reaching out before death to the only familiar person, the only one who knows what is happening.
Either way, it binds Odysseus's name to this decision forever.
May a leader conceal that some will die in order to keep everyone rowing?
This epic gives no universal answer that can be detached from particular circumstances.
Sometimes telling the truth is the minimum respect owed to a person.
Sometimes telling it immediately would deprive everyone of a chance to escape.
What must never be left out is this:
Concealment should not make those kept uninformed disappear from the decision.
If they cannot take part beforehand, the decision-maker has all the more reason to acknowledge afterward:
Who did not know.
Who bore the burden.
What truly could not be avoided.
What remained a choice I made.
Scylla takes six men.
Charybdis does not swallow the whole ship.
This shows that the route has been traversed.
But it does not turn six cries into a cost that numbers have fully explained.

*Textual basis: Homer, Odyssey, Book 12. Circe explains the two routes, past rocks that clash together or past Scylla and Charybdis, explicitly advising a swift passage close to Scylla because “mourning six aboard” is better than losing everyone. When Odysseus asks whether he can fight, Circe says that Scylla cannot be fought and that lingering will cost another six men (approximately 12.55–126). Odysseus first tells the crew that divine prophecy should not be known to just one or two, and makes full arrangements for the danger of the Sirens (approximately 12.153–200). When smoke and huge waves frighten the crew into dropping their oars, he encourages them and orders the helmsman close to the cliff, but explicitly conceals Scylla, fearing they will stop rowing and hide in the hold (approximately 12.201–232). He also defies the advice not to arm himself, taking up spears to search for Scylla; while the crew watches Charybdis, Scylla takes six of the strongest companions, who call Odysseus's name as they die (approximately 12.233–259). This essay does not portray Odysseus as arbitrarily naming six people for sacrifice, nor does it make the danger of both routes automatically absolve his decision to conceal information.*
